best_field_traits: Perennial rosette-grass; spring and late-season branched phases differ.
Vernal culms commonly have 4–7 thin stem leaves, often relatively narrow (approximately 1.3–5.5 mm broad in Central Texas treatment).
Upper leaf surface often finely hairy, underside much less hairy; margin and lower blade may carry a few long hairs with swollen bases.
True ligule often very short (~0.25–0.5 mm), requiring a macro view.
Open ovoid spring panicle; stalked/terminal obovoid spikelets roughly 3–3.5 mm.
Individual spikelets are awnless, with a lower sterile floret and fertile upper floret; precise glume characters need magnification.
crew_field_check: Start from the same rooted clump; note spring vs late-season growth.
Expose the collar and photograph the true ligule with a ruler; separate the blade-base cilia from collar hairs.
Measure at least three mature spikelets and examine glumes under magnification.
If collar or spikelet anatomy is absent, label as provisional Dichanthelium sp.
what_to_photograph_for_confirmation: Narrow vernal leaves in profile with ruler
close upper and lower blade surfaces
intact mature spikelet and separated glumes with calibrated microscope.

confused_with: other Dichanthelium species (not yet represented in this learner)
comparisons.key_distinctions: D. oligosanthes has similarly sized spikelets, so don't separate them by seedhead size alone; the narrow thin blade and much shorter ligule are especially worth recording. D. lindheimeri commonly has far smaller spikelets. D. commutatum often has larger broad-based stem leaves and minute/absent true ligule; when uncertain, photograph an intact specimen and use a regional Dichanthelium key.
